Assignment 3:

1- Build a grid of hexagonal cells: Size 10, 15 Ex, 15 Ex

2- Right-Click on the C OUTPUT and select "Flatten".

3- Use a (2-True/2-False) pattern to cull cells.

4- Extract the center points' coordinates of the resultant cells.

5- Select only the ones with the same X value of your choice (take a look at the X vlues and pick one value).

6- Jitter the resultant Points.

7- Organize them from smallest to largest Y value.

8- Find the length of the List of Points and split the List in half.

Extra step:
9- Select the cells belonging to the first half as of step (8) and extrude them by their area value in the Z direction.

1- Lists:

- Lists are some of Grasshopper's most powerful features. Lists are as their name suggests, lists of information.

- Grasshopper provides many tools to manipulate lists and use them parametrically.

- Let us generate a list of 10 numbers, starting from 1 with a step size of 1.

- "Series" component will help us do this.

- Plug a "Note" at the OUTPUT and check the information generated.

- Notice that the very first item on the right side is 1.0, however its order inside the List is 0!

This is how Grasshopper orders things or items, the first item of anthing has the order of 0, the second one has the order of 1, and so on.

- Notice as well that the 10th item inside the List has the 9th order.

- Notice the shape of the wire going out from the S OUTPUT, it is a double line. Wires what contain Lists appear as double lines.

2- Lists:

- Let us see how we can use Lists.

- Go to the tab "Sets", then "List".

- You will find here most of the components that help you manipulate Lists.

- We will discover the most useful components as we progress in this workshop...

- One of the most usedul components is "List Item", which allows you to select an item from a List.

- The "i" INPUT is the index of the item. The index is actually the order as we have seen previously.

The first index of any List is 0, and so on.

The last index of any List is -1, and so on.

4- Lists: Culling

- In Grasshopper, culling means removing.

- Try the component "Cull Index" and cull the 5th item (which is the number 6).

- The resultant List has now 9 items, starting with index 0 and ending with index 8. But the number 6 is not there anymore, it has been removed from the List.

5- Lists: More components

- The following components are often used in Grasshopper. Use the previous List generated by the Series and try:
- "List Length"
- "Insert Items"
- "Replace Items"
- "Reverse List"
- "Shift List"
- "Sort List"
- "Jitter"
- "Split List"
- "Partition List"

Practical Example:

1- Grid of squarish cells.

2- Use the "Boundary" component to make surfaces out of the cells.

3- Get the center point of each cell using the "Area" component.

4- Extract the XYZ information from the center points.

5- Select only the ones with the Y = 15.

7- Jitter the resultant List.

6- Organize (sort) these ones from smallest to largest X value.

7- Back to step 2, randomly cull 25 surfaces.

8- Back to step 2, use a pattern to cull surfaces.

9- Back to step 2, find the length of the List of surfaces and split the List in half parametrically.

3- Lists: Wrapping

- Wrapping means that the List starts again at the end without stopping.

- The below List has 10 items, first index is 0 and last index is 9.

- Try to choose the 10th index with the "List Item" component.

- The "List Item" component has a BOOLEAN INPUT "W".

- In Grasshopper, BOOLEAN does not mean geometry merge as in other software, it rather means "true" or "false".

- In this case, let us see what happens when we choose the item with 10th idex (which does not exist since the last item has the index 9).

- With a "True" BOOLEAN, the List seems to loop and start again from the beginning, hence the 10th item is 1.

- With a "False" BOOLEAN, the List gives a "null" result. In other words, it is saying that there is no 10th item to be displayed.
